newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.S. moves to spur WTO financial services talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. moves to spur WTO financial services talks.

text.p: The United States moved Monday to spur World Trade Organisation (WTO) talks on a global pact to open up financial services by holding out the prospect of equal access to its market for all other countries in the body.

But the new U.S. offer was coupled with a warning that developing countries would have to pledge to liberalise their markets to make a deal possible. The offer came as a fresh round of talks got under way.
A U.S. official in Geneva told reporters Washington was "very disappointed" that a Japanese offer made on Friday did not reflect accords between the two countries in opening up the insurance sector.
A statement in Washington said the U.S. offer would provide "substantially full market access and national treatment to foreign banking, securities and insurance service suppliers."
Signed by Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin and Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky, it repeated earlier U.S. calls for similar moves by the major developing countries.

"To make this offer permanent it is critical that our trading partners, especially the key emerging markets, submit significantly improved offers that establish a level playing field for U.S. firms to compete effectively," they declared.

The U.S. official in Geneva said the package "fully incorporates financial sector liberalisation undertaken in our market," the world's largest, and included "important improvements" to the Washington offer presently on the table.

Delivery of the package to the WTO followed new offers by Japan on Friday and by the European Union two weeks ago. Canada, the fourth top trade power, was expected to offer its latest package by Wednesday.
Washington pulled out of the last bid to reach a pact in 1995, arguing that proposals from key developing countries at the time were not sufficient.
Speaking to reporters on condition of anonymity, the U.S. official in Geneva said Washington was disappointed many other countries in the talks had not tabled new offers by Monday.
All WTO members had agreed in principle last month to have fresh packages ready for this week's round of talks in Geneva.

"We look to them now to put their offers on the table so we can begin intensive negotiations," the official said. Serious bargaining is not expected before autumn with the deadline for an agreement in December.

When the 1995 talks were on the verge of collapse, the EU convinced other countries to agree to an interim deal excluding the United States. But that accord expires at year-end and there is no support for its continuation. Officials said a long-term pact is of little value if it does not cover the United States.
The U.S. official said Washington wanted better offers from major Asian and Latin American countries but also wanted improvements from African nations and ex-communist states in Europe.

Senior U.S. trade negotiator Jeffrey Lang and other officials will tour Seoul, Manila, Jakarta, New Delhi and other capitals in August "in an effort to push Asian countries forward," the official said.
